intro: Scarlatti’s Sonata in D major, K. 119, an Allegro, opens with a few plain notes in D major and then fills the keyboard with dissonant chords. Marcelle Meyer plays the sonata’s leaps, trills and clashing chords on the piano.

sections.label: A · D major, leaps and trills
sections.mNote: A short opening phrase expands into dense chords

sections.label: A · Opening material in D major
sections.mNote: The repeat moves directly from A major back to D major.

sections.label: B · Second half over A bass, flats
sections.mNote: B♭ enters at the opening of the second half.

sections.label: B · Second half, ending in D major
sections.mNote: The piano returns to A after the D-major ending.

sections.label: Coda · Running figures in D major
sections.mNote: The closing figures return to D major.

relations.label: The first half repeats
relations.basis: The sonata has two repeated halves; the first moves from D towards A. The measured pair falls inside that first half and its repeat, marked near 68 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.967, sustained 48.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 65.5 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The second half repeats
relations.basis: The second half returns towards D and is repeated near 204 s. These excerpts compare its later phrases, not the first half or a later Classical sonata-form recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.941, sustained 42.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 72 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening bars
cues.text: The right hand begins with a few plain quavers above a D-major chord and reaches higher up the keyboard with each phrase. The left hand then takes up the running notes as well.
cues.evidence: Scarlatti, Sonata K. 119, edited by Pierre Gouin (Les Éditions Outremontaises, 2013), bars 1–17. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dissonant repeated chords
cues.text: The single lines give way to thick chords. Scarlatti adds dissonant notes to repeated chords, then returns both hands to running figures. The dissonances belong to the harmony as written.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, first half, especially bars 55–72: repeated chords with added dissonant notes, followed by running figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Repeat of the first half
cues.text: The first half closes in A major. Its repeat returns the piano to the opening in D major, and then the leaps and crowded chords begin again. Both halves of the sonata have repeat signs.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, first-half repeat after bar 95, returning to bar 1; the second repeat follows bar 207. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Move to Seville, 1729
cues.text: In 1729 Maria Bárbara left Portugal for Spain, married to the Spanish heir. Scarlatti followed his royal pupil to Seville and continued as her private music master. In 1733 the court moved back to Madrid.
cues.evidence: Cristina Fernandes, Scarlatti, Giuseppe Domenico, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 91 (2018): the move to Seville in 1729 and Madrid in 1733. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Opening of the second half
cues.text: The second half begins over an A bass, with B♭ in the upper line at bar 97 and further chromatic changes after it. The repeated notes and trills come from the first half.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, bars 96–107: A in the bass, with B♭ in the melody at bar 97 and subsequent chromatic changes. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeat of the second half
cues.text: The second half closes with a cadence in D major. In the Gouin edition the repeat sign at the end of bar 207 sends the player back to bar 96, to the A in the bass and the flats. The hands play that crowded passage a second time.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, repeat at the end of bar 207, returning to bar 96. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in D major
cues.text: The closing figures run across the keyboard in D major. Trills break into the runs, and the hands exchange high and low notes before a final descent to the tonic chord. Scarlatti places a fermata over the last D.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, bars 183–207: running and trilled figures, final D-major cadence and fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A major returns to D
transitions.from: A · D major, leaps and trills
transitions.to: A · Opening material in D major
transitions.how: The first half ends on A after its closing runs and trills. The repeat goes straight back to the opening D-major chord and its three-quaver melody (bars 91–95 leading to bars 1–6 in the Gouin edition, 2013).
transitions.evidence: Gouin edition (2013), bars 91–95 and the return to bars 1–6. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf

transitions.title: B♭ over the A bass
transitions.from: A · Opening material in D major
transitions.to: B · Second half over A bass, flats
transitions.how: The first half closes in A major, and the second half begins over an A in the bass. In the next bar the right hand plays B♭. The bass stays on A while the upper notes move chromatically. Trills and repeated figures continue the phrase.

transitions.title: Final D major cadence to second-half repeat
transitions.from: B · Second half over A bass, flats
transitions.to: B · Second half, ending in D major
transitions.how: The cadence reaches D major and pauses. The repeat sign then returns to the opening of the second half, with its A bass and the quick B♭ above it. There is no linking phrase, and the key changes at the restart.
transitions.evidence: Gouin edition (2013), final bars 201–207 and return to bars 96–99. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf

transitions.title: Into the closing D-major runs
transitions.from: B · Second half, ending in D major
transitions.to: Coda · Running figures in D major
transitions.how: Repeated-note figures lead into the final runs in D major. The bass alternates D with its dominant, A, and the hands jump between octaves and exchange the quick notes. A last descending run reaches the held D-major chord at the end, marked with a fermata.

composer.epithet: A royal teacher known for his keyboard sonatas.
facts: Alessandro Scarlatti’s sixth child; born in 1685, the year of Bach and Handel
Maria Bárbara of Portugal, later Queen of Spain; he served her until his death
Naples and Rome; Lisbon from 1719; Spain from 1729
555 in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; most survive in manuscript copies
composer.background:
On 30 May 1705 Alessandro Scarlatti wrote to Ferdinando de’ Medici about his nineteen-year-old son Domenico: “This son is an eagle whose wings have grown; he must not idle in the nest, and I must not prevent his flight.” Domenico already held a post as organist at the royal chapel in Naples and had written operas. His father sent him north towards Venice, by way of Florence, with this recommendation. Domenico later settled much farther from home, as teacher to a Portuguese princess whose marriage took them both to Spain.

Domenico was born in Naples on 26 October 1685, the same year as J. S. Bach and Handel, the sixth of Alessandro’s ten children. His family included singers as well as composers, and several of them worked in opera. He became a salaried royal organist at fifteen. In Rome he served Maria Casimira, the widowed Queen of Poland, who maintained a theatre in her Palazzo Zuccari. Scarlatti supplied her with seven operas between 1710 and 1714, working with the poet Carlo Sigismondo Capece and the stage designer Filippo Juvarra.
